newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FUND VIEW - India bulls ignore gloomy backdrop.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW - India bulls ignore gloomy backdrop.

text.p: Indian stocks will rebound on increased foreign investment next year even though the country faces one of the most uncertain economic outlooks in the world, fund managers based in Hong Kong said.

"Global asset allocators will be putting money into India next year because on a value basis it's screamingly cheap. It's half the value of Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and it's much cheaper than Thailand, which remains a disaster in my view," said Christopher Wood, Asia and emerging markets strategist for Peregrine Investment.
Bombay stocks have fallen 30 percent so far this year reflecting widespread nervousness about the possibility of an economic slowdown extending into a full recession.
Bombay's SENSEX closed 0.89 points up at 2881.15 on Friday, recovering from a year-low of 2745 reached on December 4. The index hit a year-high of 4069 on June 18.

"The economy is slow, rates are down, but the liquidity situation is improving," Wood said last week. "Indian markets are cheaper than at any time since deregulation in 1991. We've had the post-deregulation boom in India. Now we're at a bust."
Others were not quite so enthusiastic.
In a recent report, ING Barings warned against bottom fishing under any circumstances.
"We believe the market has sensed the impending danger in economic and corporate performance but has not sufficiently discounted it due to a lack of conclusive evidence," it said.
"It is advisable to avoid bottom-fishing and to delay further investment, at least until the grim realities in the capital market environment have been adequately factored in."
Sliding corporate earnings, a gross fiscal deficit among the highest of the decade and an internal debt trap have pushed India to the brink of a major shake- out, ING Barings said.
Concern about the Indian government's commitment to continued economic reform was cited as a reason to steer clear by HSBC Asset Management.

"We got India wrong," director Graham Muirhead said, candidly. "We bought earlier this year. We thought earnings growth was strong and valuations attractive, but in fact earnings were very disappointing and politically, the new government doesn't seem as keen to continue the reform process. So we'll wait and see in India."
But others untouched by the meltdown so far were obviously considering reweighting this year in favour of India regardless of the poor economic outlook.
"This is probably the year India bottoms, in stock market terms," said Christopher Day, joint managing director at Thornton Management (Asia) Ltd.
"That doesn't necessarily mean you'll get levitation on the other side, but from a stock market point of view, it's unlikely to get too much worse. 1997 will be the year it bottoms out."
